I have been farming this land in Quzhou for over fifty years. My family plot is about 3 mu — my son handles the heavier mechanized work now, but the decisions are still mine.

The North China Plain double-cropping rotation is what I know and what this land demands: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same ground. I would not experiment with cotton or vegetables at my age and with my plot size. The market infrastructure here is built around grain, and I know the timing, the inputs, and the risks by heart.

For wheat, I will use an improved variety — likely one from the county agricultural station's subsidized program, something with good lodging resistance since I cannot always respond quickly to weather. I will keep irrigations to three: sowing water to ensure germination, jointing stage, and heading stage. Hebei's groundwater extraction quotas have tightened, and I was already using less water than my neighbors a decade ago. My nitrogen rate I have gradually reduced from what I used in my fifties — the soil tests the extension station ran a few years ago showed I had been over-applying. Twelve kilograms per mu total, split between basal and one topdressing at jointing, is right for my yield target.

For maize, I direct-seed into the wheat stubble in mid-June without tillage — saves fuel, saves my son's time, and residue retention is good for soil moisture going into summer. Summer rainfall in Quzhou is variable; I budget for one irrigation but may need two if July is dry. I spray herbicide once at emergence and watch for corn borer, one pesticide pass mid-season.

I expect 450 kg/mu wheat and 550 kg/mu maize. These are not record yields, but they are honest and reliable for a 3-mu plot managed carefully by an old man and his son.
